transcript.text: I think my washer dryer has a fault - I put it on just a drying programme with dry-ish clothes and I can hear water running into it and draining the whole time. Surely it shouldn't use water to dry? It's a Beko.

It does sound odd, but in most cases that's exactly what a washer-dryer is meant to do. Most washer-dryers, Beko's included, are condenser dryers. There's no vent hose, so they need another way to get rid of the moisture coming out of the clothes. They do it by trickling a small amount of cold water through the condensing duct while drying. The warm, damp air passes over it, the moisture turns back into water, and the drain pump runs every so often to pump it all away. So a quiet hiss of water coming in and the pump kicking in now and then, all the way through the dry, is normal. It's also why the cold tap has to stay on while it dries. 1. Look through the door glass part-way through. You shouldn't see water sitting in the bottom of the drum, and the clothes shouldn't be getting wetter. If the drum is filling to a visible level, it's more likely running a wash or rinse stage. That would point to the programme selection rather than a fault, so check a drying-only programme is chosen with no wash or spin option added. 2. Gently feel the door glass or the top of the machine after 20 to 30 minutes. It should feel warm. 3. Check the result at the end. If the clothes come out dry or nearly dry, everything is working as designed. 4. Look for any water on the floor while it dries. A leak would suggest the condensed water isn't draining properly. The usual culprits are fluff in the pump filter at the bottom front, or a kinked drain hose. Unplug it, put towels and a shallow tray down, and unscrew the filter slowly to clean it. If it heats, drains without leaking and the clothes come out dry, you can relax: it's simply how it works.

Thank you, that's helpful. I had a look: there's no water in the drum and the clothes aren't getting wet, there's no leak on the floor, and the clothes do come out dry at the end. I didn't think to feel the door glass, so I can't say whether it was warm.

That all points firmly to normal behaviour. There's no water building up in the drum, no leak, and the clothes come out dry, so the condensing water is coming in, doing its job and being pumped away properly. Don't worry about the door glass. The clothes coming out dry already proves it's heating. If the heater weren't working, you'd get warm-free, damp clothes at the end no matter how long it ran. The things that would make it a fault are:
1. Water visibly filling the drum during a drying-only programme, or clothes getting wetter. That would mean a wash or rinse stage is running, or the water isn't draining.
2. Water on the floor while drying. That's usually fluff blocking the pump filter or a kinked drain hose.
3. Clothes still damp at the end of a load that's within the dry capacity, which is usually about half the wash capacity.
4. Water running in when the machine is off or idle. That would point to an inlet valve sticking open, and it's worth an engineer. One bit of upkeep: fluff from drying ends up in the pump filter at the bottom front, so clean it every month or two if you dry often (unplug the machine, and have towels and a shallow tray ready). That keeps the condensing water draining freely. Otherwise, you can carry on using it as normal.

candidates: Normal condenser drying: a cold-water trickle condenses the moisture and the pump drains it away (high)
Wash or rinse stage running instead of drying-only (programme selection) (low)
Drain or condensing water path fault, such as a blocked pump filter or drain hose (low)
